title: Fragments of Horror
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Junji Ito's eight-story horror anthology: a husband trapped in a futon by hallucinations, a woman who merges with a historic wooden house, a fortune teller who collects severed heads, a wife who learns she is a lingering 'afterimage' of the dead, a girl who begs to be dissected, a woman who feeds a stranded man his own flesh, a novelist who imprisons people to study their quirks, and a caretaker who whispers instructions to an anxious girl even after death (Wikipedia; Viz blurb via AniList; MU).
life_message: No single message; reviewers note recurring stories of women betrayed by unfaithful men and freed by uncanny female figures.

content.note: Garroting, severed heads, stabbing with scissors, dissection, flesh-eating (Wikipedia); AniList Gore 82%, Body Horror 80%.
Reviewers call it gruesome and Lovecraftian (Wikipedia); AniList Tragedy, Cosmic Horror.
Woman rubbing herself naked against walls, affairs, a one-night stand (Wikipedia); AniList Nudity 60%; Viz blurb says 'erotic'.
Loud-mouthed, mean-spirited novelist (Wikipedia); detail not sourced.
Hallucinogenic mold; a character drinks to unconsciousness and is imprisoned (Wikipedia).
Severe anxiety (aboulomania), trauma, abusive partner, a girl wanting to be dissected (Wikipedia; MU Hallucination/s).
Adapted in Junji Ito Collection anime (Wikipedia).

dominant: Uncanny horror; betrayal and infidelity; grotesque made beautiful

frames.aligns: 'Gentle Goodbye' treats grief and letting go of the dead tenderly (Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Erotic grotesque imagery, nudity and gore; infidelity as recurring premise.

frames.aligns: Shows the ruin of infidelity and passions.
frames.concerns: Demons, ghostly afterimages from prayer, sexual imagery.
Nudity, gore, fortune tellers and demons.
Demonic children, demon lovers, fortune-telling as horror fuel.

frames.aligns: Literary horror with some humane stories.
Women confronting men's faithlessness (TCJ reviewer via Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: A cross-dressing villain may read as a stereotype (Wikipedia).

frames.aligns: Attachment and letting go of the dead explored.
Female agency themes noted by reviewers.
frames.concerns: Cross-dressing villain trope; abuse; sexualized imagery.
Spirits of the dead as real; gore; nudity.
Fortune teller and witches as murderers.

frames.aligns: A historic house as a living presence.
frames.concerns: Defilement of a cultural property; death imagery.
Behavioral therapy then murder by suggestion.

frames.aligns: Grotesque art; liberated antagonists (TCJ via Wikipedia).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wronged women's uncanny retribution recurs (TCJ, Comics & Cola via Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Liberated, uncaring female antagonists (TCJ via Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family houses and in-law clans feature ('Wooden Spirit', 'Gentle Goodbye').

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: No consistent hierarchy; town association mocks a victim.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Family prayers create afterimages; fortune tellers, demons (Wikipedia).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival of horrors, but a novelist's art at any cost.

folkways.japan: A designated Tangible Cultural Property, family prayer rites for the dead and a josei magazine audience shape these stories.

delivery.evidence: The Guardian notes Ito avoids being political; TCJ sees themes of faithless men but doubts they are sincere (via Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Reviewers read recurring gender themes into the stories, but the book does not argue for them.

winners_losers: Unfaithful men and curious victims usually suffer; uncanny female figures often prevail. Sympathy goes to wronged women, per reviewers.
to_verify: Explicitness of nudity in 'Wooden Spirit' (AniList Nudity 60%)
